lead: Mesh analysis turns Kirchhoff's voltage law into a short set of simultaneous equations. Every window of a flat (planar) circuit gets its own circulating mesh current, and you write one KVL equation per window. When a current source sits on a branch shared by two meshes, the two are treated together as a supermesh. Mesh analysis suits circuits with many series elements and voltage sources, such as battery packs and bridges.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws, and the passive sign convention (circuit elements and laws).

sections.h3: Meshes, mesh currents and how many equations

blocks.text: A circuit is planar when you can draw it on paper with no branch crossing another. A mesh is a loop that has no other loop inside it: one window of the drawing. A circuit with b branches and n nodes has exactly b − n + 1 meshes, so mesh analysis needs b − n + 1 equations.

Give each mesh a clockwise current i₁, i₂, and so on. An outside branch belongs to one mesh, so its current is that mesh current. A shared branch carries two mesh currents in opposite directions, so its current is the difference. In the top circuit of the figure the 4 Ω resistor is shared: its downward current is i₁ − i₂.

Why it works: KCL is satisfied automatically, because each mesh current enters and leaves every node it passes. Only KVL is left to write, one equation per mesh, and each equation contains only mesh currents.

sections.h3: Writing the mesh equations by inspection

items: Check that the circuit is planar, number its meshes and draw every mesh current clockwise.

For mesh k, walk round clockwise and add the voltage drops: each resistor in the mesh gives R × i<sub>k</sub>, and a shared resistor R gives R × (i<sub>k</sub> − i<sub>j</sub>), where j is the neighbouring mesh.
Put the sources on the right side: a source counts positive when the walk goes from its − terminal to its + terminal (a rise in the clockwise direction).
Solve the equations, then find branch currents and voltages from the mesh currents.

blocks.text: Together the equations form R i = v. The diagonal entry Rkk, the self-resistance, is the sum of the resistances in mesh k. The off-diagonal entry Rkj is minus the mutual resistance shared by meshes k and j. The right side vk is the net source rise in mesh k. With independent sources only the matrix is symmetric, a quick check on your working.

Dependent sources. A controlled source stays in the KVL equation, with its value written in mesh currents: in the top circuit 2iₓ = 2(i₁ − i₂). Move every mesh-current term to the left. The matrix is then usually not symmetric, which is correct.
A current source fixes a current, but its voltage is set by the rest of the circuit, so a KVL equation through it would carry a new unknown.

items: Source on an outside branch (in one mesh only): it fixes that mesh current directly, for example i₃ = −2 A if a 2 A source points against the clockwise direction. One equation fewer to solve.
Source on a shared branch: join the two meshes into a supermesh. Write one KVL equation round their outer path, leaving out the shared branch, plus the constraint the source sets.

blocks.text: Sign rule for the constraint: compare the source arrow with each mesh current where it passes through the shared branch. In the bottom circuit of the figure the 3 A source points up. Clockwise i₂ goes up through that branch and clockwise i₁ goes down, so the upward current is i₂ − i₁ = 3 A. A resistor in series with the current source (the 5 Ω) carries the fixed 3 A and lies off the supermesh path, so it never enters the KVL equation.
The same steps work for AC circuits with impedances in place of resistances (see applying network theorems to AC circuits).

examples.question: In the top circuit of Figure 2.1.1 (24 V source, 2 Ω top-left and top-right, 4 Ω in the shared branch, and a controlled source 2iₓ, + at the top, in the right branch, where iₓ is the downward current in the 4 Ω), find the mesh currents and iₓ, and check the power balance.
steps: Draw i₁ (left) and i₂ (right) clockwise. The downward current in the 4 Ω resistor is iₓ = i₁ − i₂, so the controlled source is 2(i₁ − i₂) V.
Mesh 1, walking clockwise: the 24 V source is a rise; drops are 2i₁ and 4(i₁ − i₂). So 2i₁ + 4(i₁ − i₂) = 24, that is 6i₁ − 4i₂ = 24.

Mesh 2, clockwise: 2i₂ in the top-right resistor, 2(i₁ − i₂) down through the controlled source from + to −, and 4(i₂ − i₁) up through the 4 Ω. So 2i₂ + 2(i₁ − i₂) + 4(i₂ − i₁) = 0, that is −2i₁ + 4i₂ = 0.
From mesh 2, i₁ = 2i₂. Substitute in mesh 1: 6(2i₂) − 4i₂ = 24, so 8i₂ = 24 and i₂ = 3 A. Then i₁ = 6 A.
iₓ = i₁ − i₂ = 3 A, so the controlled source is 2 × 3 = 6 V.
Power check: the 24 V source delivers 24 × 6 = 144 W. Absorbed: 6² × 2 = 72 W, 3² × 4 = 36 W, 3² × 2 = 18 W, and the controlled source takes 3 A into its + terminal, 6 × 3 = 18 W. Total 144 W.
examples.answer: i₁ = 6 A, i₂ = 3 A, iₓ = 3 A (controlled source 6 V); 144 W delivered and 144 W absorbed.

examples.question: In the bottom circuit of Figure 2.1.1 (24 V source, 2 Ω top-left, 5 Ω in series with a 3 A source pointing up in the shared branch, 3 Ω top-right, 1 Ω on the right), find the mesh currents and the voltage across the current source.
steps: The 3 A source is on the shared branch, so meshes 1 and 2 form a supermesh.
Constraint: the source points up; i₂ flows up and i₁ flows down in that branch, so i₂ − i₁ = 3 A.
Supermesh KVL round the outer path (24 V source, 2 Ω, 3 Ω, 1 Ω): 2i₁ + 3i₂ + 1i₂ = 24, that is 2i₁ + 4i₂ = 24. The 5 Ω is not on this path.
Substitute i₂ = i₁ + 3: 2i₁ + 4i₁ + 12 = 24, so 6i₁ = 12, i₁ = 2 A and i₂ = 5 A.
Voltage of the top junction above the bottom wire: 24 − 2 × 2 = 20 V (check from the right: 5 × (3 + 1) = 20 V).
The 3 A flows up through the 5 Ω, so the bottom of the 5 Ω is 5 × 3 = 15 V above its top: the current source's upper terminal is at 20 + 15 = 35 V. The source has 35 V across it, upper end positive.
Power check: the 24 V source delivers 24 × 2 = 48 W and the current source delivers 35 × 3 = 105 W, total 153 W. Absorbed: 2² × 2 + 5² × 3 + 5² × 1 + 3² × 5 = 8 + 75 + 25 + 45 = 153 W.
examples.answer: i₁ = 2 A, i₂ = 5 A; the current source has 35 V across it and delivers 105 W.

traps: Writing KVL through a current source as if its voltage were zero. Use the supermesh, or fix the mesh current for an outside branch.
Getting the constraint sign backwards. In worked example 2 it is i₂ − i₁ = 3 A; i₁ − i₂ = 3 A solves a different circuit.
Putting the resistor in series with the current source into the supermesh equation. It is off the outer path.
Writing the mutual term with a plus sign. With all mesh currents clockwise, a shared resistor always enters as R(i<sub>k</sub> − i<sub>j</sub>) in mesh k.
Expecting a symmetric matrix when a dependent source is present, and 'correcting' a correct answer.

quiz.q: Define a mesh and state the condition a circuit must meet for the window method of mesh analysis.
quiz.a: A mesh is a loop that contains no other loop inside it. The circuit must be planar: drawable with no branch crossing another.

quiz.q: Why does a shared resistor enter the mesh matrix with a minus sign when all mesh currents are clockwise?
quiz.a: The two clockwise mesh currents pass through the shared resistor in opposite directions, so its drop in mesh k is R(i<sub>k</sub> − i<sub>j</sub>). The coefficient of i<sub>j</sub> is −R.

quiz.q: A planar circuit has 6 branches and 4 nodes. How many mesh equations are needed?
In worked example 2, the 3 A source is turned round to point down. Write the constraint and find i₁ and i₂.
quiz.a: Now i₁ − i₂ = 3 A. With 2i₁ + 4i₂ = 24: 2(i₂ + 3) + 4i₂ = 24, so 6i₂ = 18, i₂ = 3 A and i₁ = 6 A.

quiz.q: In worked example 1, the coefficient matrix is [6 −4; −2 4]. Explain why it is not symmetric, and show that mesh 2's equation still gives the right i₂.
quiz.a: The controlled source adds 2(i₁ − i₂) to mesh 2 only, changing the i₁ coefficient there from −4 to −2 and the i₂ coefficient from 6 to 4. Check: −2(6) + 4(3) = 0, so i₁ = 6 A, i₂ = 3 A satisfy mesh 2.

beyond: Circuit simulators such as SPICE do not use mesh analysis; they build modified nodal analysis equations, because every circuit has nodes but not every circuit is planar. Loop equations chosen from a graph's tree (tie-set matrices) extend mesh analysis to any circuit. Search for 'tie-set matrix' and 'modified nodal analysis'.

figure.caption: Top: the two-mesh circuit of worked example 1; the controlled source 2iₓ depends on the current iₓ = i₁ − i₂ in the 4 Ω resistor, so the second mesh equation is not symmetric with the first. Bottom: worked example 2, where the 3 A source sits in the shared branch; one KVL around the dashed outer loop plus i₂ − i₁ = 3 A replaces the two mesh equations.
